title: How GPS knows where you are
performance: Explain to a colleague, in a few sentences, how a phone turns satellite signals into a position: timed broadcasts, distance from travel time, intersecting spheres, a fourth satellite for the phone's clock, and the relativity correction to the satellites' clocks.

audience.assumed_prior: Uses a map app daily; knows satellites orbit Earth and that nothing is faster than light; no geometry or physics beyond school memories.
audience.why: Corporate employees with no technical brief; the request asks for a general explainer, so every term is shown before it is named.
audience.motivation: Curiosity about a tool they rely on every day, and the pleasure of an elegant answer they can repeat.
audience.context: Watched at a desk or on a phone between tasks, sound on, captions available; one sitting of about four minutes.

strategy.name: question_led
strategy.rationale: The topic has one genuine puzzle at its heart (the phone sends nothing, yet knows where it is), and the facts (F1 to F16) answer it as a chain where each step raises the next question: what is broadcast, how far, where exactly, why the clock fails, why the satellite clocks drift.
strategy.signature_move: Ask the next question in the phone's own case, show the mechanism running on screen, then name the idea just used in one plain sentence.

misconceptions.belief: The phone sends a signal up and the satellites track it
misconceptions.why_tempting: Most everyday wireless (calls, messages) is two-way, and 'satellite tracking' is a common phrase
School geometry and many simplified explanations stop at three circles

misconceptions.belief: Relativity is a theoretical curiosity with no practical effect
misconceptions.why_tempting: It sounds remote from daily life

hook.sketch: Night, a city, a phone opens a map and the blue dot appears. Pull back to orbit: the phone has told no one where it is. So how does it know?

arc.promise: In four minutes: the whole chain from a satellite's broadcast to that blue dot, and why it all comes down to keeping time honest.
arc.bridge_from_prior: You already know two things that do the work: satellites circle the Earth, and nothing is faster than light. GPS is built from just those two.

sections.goal: the viewer can state what each satellite broadcasts and that the phone only listens
concepts: satellite broadcasts its position (F1)
and the time of sending from atomic clocks (F2)
the receiver is passive (F3)
about two dozen satellites, about 20,200 km up, about 12 h orbit (F17, F18)
sections.carrier: Earth and the constellation on visible orbits; one satellite's broadcast as an expanding wavefront carrying a position and a time stamp toward the phone

sections.goal: the viewer can explain how travel time becomes a distance and a sphere of possible positions
concepts: radio travels at about 300,000 km/s (F4)
distance = travel time x speed of light (F5)
about 0.07 s from overhead (F6)
one distance = a sphere around the satellite (F7)
sections.carrier: the signal travelling satellite to phone with a timer on the phone, then the distance swept out as a sphere (a circle in the flat picture) centred on the satellite

sections.goal: the viewer can apply the intersecting-circles picture to show why a fourth satellite is needed to fix the phone's clock
concepts: two spheres meet in a circle, three in two points (F7)
in principle three would do with a perfect clock (F8)
the phone's clock is cheap quartz, every distance shifted the same (F9)
four unknowns, four satellites (F10)
sections.carrier: one diagram that builds: circles added one at a time until one point lights; then the phone's clock shown off, all circles swollen by the same amount and failing to meet, and a fourth circle pulling them back to one point

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why the satellites' clocks need a relativity correction and what happens without it
concepts: 1 microsecond of error ~ 300 m (F11)
speed slows orbit clocks about 7 microseconds a day (F12)
weaker gravity speeds them about 45 a day (F13)
net gain about 38 a day (F14)
uncorrected: roughly 10 km a day of build-up (F15)
clock rate set lower before launch (F16)
sections.carrier: two clocks side by side, ground and orbit, drifting apart as the day counter runs; the blue dot sliding away across the map; then the pre-set rate and the clocks back in step

sections.goal: the viewer can summarize the full chain as one timing story
concepts: the chain recapped: broadcast, travel time, spheres, fourth satellite, corrected clocks
the position is an estimate with real-world error (F20)
sections.carrier: the diagram returns and replays in brief, then pulls back to the city and the blue dot

arc.payoff: The blue dot is the answer to a timing problem solved continuously: listen, time, intersect, fix the clock, and trust clocks that were set for relativity before they left the ground.

practice_ladder.what: The narrator walks one phone through the full chain on screen (s1 to s3).
pause_predict after three circles meet: with the phone's clock off, what would you need? The viewer predicts; the fourth satellite is the reveal.
Transfer task: retell the chain to a colleague in four steps.

slowdown_at: s3 the fourth satellite and the clock error
s4 the two relativity effects pulling in opposite directions

recall_moments.where: inside s3, after the three circles fail to meet because the phone clock is off, before the fourth satellite appears
recall_moments.prompt: The phone's clock is off, so every circle is wrong by the same amount. What would fix it?
Remember the timer that turned travel time into distance? Now ask how good the satellites' own clocks are.
The chain in one breath: broadcast, travel time, spheres, a fourth satellite, corrected clocks.

transfer_tasks: Explain to a colleague why a phone needs at least four satellites, not three.
When the blue dot jumps in a city of tall buildings, name which step of the chain is being disturbed (signals reflected or blocked, F20).

gagne.attention: hook: the blue dot appearing and the question of how
gagne.recall_prior: bridge_from_prior: satellites orbit, light is fastest
gagne.guidance: signature_move and the one building diagram in s2 and s3
gagne.feedback: the reveal of the fourth satellite explains why the clock error is shared by every circle
gagne.assess: absent as a formal test: a four-minute explainer within the stopping-check budget; the recap recall_prompt in s5 stands in
gagne.transfer: payoff, transfer_tasks, recall_prompts at s4 and s5

merrill.problem_centred: one phone's question (where am I) runs through every section
merrill.activation: bridge_from_prior and the everyday blue dot
merrill.demonstration: the mechanism shown running in s1 to s4
merrill.application: pause_predict in s3 and the retell transfer task
merrill.integration: transfer task on the blue dot jumping between tall buildings

mayer.coherence: no GPS feature list or uses; only the chain
mayer.signalling: the accent on one element at a time: the wavefront, the circle, the lit point, the clocks
mayer.redundancy: captions on; on-screen words limited to labels and numbers, not narration text
mayer.contiguity: numbers sit on the object they describe (the time stamp on the wavefront, the drift on the clock)
mayer.pre_training: s1 names the parts (satellite, broadcast, time stamp, phone) before the mechanism

arcs.attention: the hook question and the cosmic zoom from the city to orbit
arcs.relevance: the everyday blue dot they use daily
arcs.confidence: one step at a time with the same phone, each step named after it is seen
arcs.satisfaction: the chain closes on the blue dot; the relativity reveal as the elegant twist
